reasons: Lake identity gives case_name Michigan v. Chesternut, court U.S. Supreme Court, date_decided 1988-06-13, and year 1988.
Lake citations give official cite 486 U.S. 567, vendor-neutral cite 1988 U.S. LEXIS 2582, and parallel cites 108 S. Ct. 1975, 100 L. Ed. 2d 565, and 56 U.S.L.W. 4558.

defect.evidence_quote: we adhere to our traditional contextual approach, and determine only that, in this particular case, the police conduct in question did not amount to a seizure.
defect.problem: The holding overstates Chesternut as a categorical rule about police pursuit. The opinion expressly refused a bright-line rule for investigatory pursuits and limited its seizure holding to the facts of this case, though the Mendenhall objective-test clause is supported.
defect.proposed_fix: Replace with: On these facts, a brief police-car pursuit/parallel drive without sirens, commands, weapons, aggressive blocking, or control of movement was not a seizure; whether police conduct is a seizure is assessed under Mendenhall by asking whether, in all the circumstances, a reasonable person would have believed he was not free to leave.

reasons: The opinion says both parties failed by seeking bright-line rules and that the Court determined only that the conduct in this particular case did not amount to a seizure.
The supported narrower facts are: no siren or flashers, no command to halt, no weapons displayed, and no aggressive blocking or control of respondent's direction or speed.
The Mendenhall test portion is supported by the opinion's statement that seizure exists only if, in all the circumstances, a reasonable person would have believed he was not free to leave.
residual_risks: The same overbroad shorthand also appears in the treatment scope note, but treatment/currency is outside Lens A.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Use fact-specific language keyed to the police car briefly catching up and driving alongside Chesternut, not generic police pursuit.

reasons: The opinion directly concerns whether the officers' pursuit of respondent constituted a Fourth Amendment seizure of a person.
The opinion applies the Mendenhall free-to-leave test, and the lake outbound edges include United States v. Mendenhall, supporting a progeny/application role in the seizure-of-the-person doctrine.
residual_risks: No separate home-page taxonomy definition is disclosed; verdict relies on the opinion's subject matter and its application of Mendenhall.
